claims.text: Limited atomic diffusion kinetics are the dominant factor preserving a homogeneous single-phase structure in high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Limited diffusion preserves structural homogeneity by suppressing local chemical segregation and ordering.
High configurational entropy favors chemical mixing.
The initial equimolar nanoalloy has a predominantly random atomic distribution and minimal pre-existing short-range order.
Changing annealing temperature between approximately 700°C and 1100°C and changing hold time modulates atomic diffusion.
Atomic diffusion kinetics affect the formation of local chemical order or clustering.
Nanoscale constraints limit atomic mobility at elevated temperatures.
Restricted atomic mobility prevents the rapid rearrangements needed to produce observable chemical ordering or segregation.
Suppression of atomic rearrangement maintains a metastable homogeneous structure.
Longer annealing times or temperatures above a kinetic threshold enhance atomic mobility.
Enhanced atomic mobility triggers measurable local ordering and phase segregation.
At moderate temperatures and short hold times, the nanoalloy will remain nearly homogeneous and single-phase with minimal local clustering.
At higher effective temperatures or longer hold times, the nanoalloy will develop significant local chemical order or initial phase segregation.
The enhanced-mobility baseline exhibits diffusion-driven local chemical ordering or phase segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies to equimolar high-entropy nanoalloys over approximately 700°C to 1100°C.
Substantial departures from equimolar composition can alter the balance between thermodynamic mixing and diffusion kinetics.
The transition temperature and diffusion rate depend on nanoalloy composition and experimental conditions.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says that higher-temperature or longer-duration samples will show increased ordering or segregation relative to the baseline, but the baseline is itself defined as samples treated at higher temperatures or extended hold times with evident ordering or segregation. This leaves no distinct baseline for that comparison.
